common_name: Wichita Blue Juniper (Upright Silver-Blue Screening Conifer)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun; Wichita Blue is very drought tolerant once established and resents heavy, wet, poorly drained soil.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun; Wichita Blue is a Rocky Mountain juniper cultivar prized for its dense, broadly pyramidal form and intense, silvery powder-blue foliage that holds its color well through winter, when many blue conifers dull to green or purple-brown. It grows at a moderate, predictable rate into a strong architectural accent or informal screen, and its upright habit and cold hardiness make it a popular choice from the Great Plains through the upper South. Established plants are highly drought tolerant and need little maintenance beyond occasional light shearing to maintain shape, and they should be sited with good air circulation to reduce the fungal blight issues that can affect junipers in humid climates.

common_name: Blue Point Juniper (Pyramidal Blue-Green Screening Conifer)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Point tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soils better than many blue conifers, making it one of the most widely planted screening junipers in the South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Blue Point is one of the most widely planted landscape junipers, forming a dense, neatly pyramidal cone of soft, silvery blue-green foliage that requires minimal pruning to keep its naturally tidy shape. Its predictable, formal habit makes it a favorite for foundation plantings, entryway accents, and mass screening, and it tolerates heat and drought once established far better than it tolerates poorly drained, soggy soil. Give it full sun and good air circulation to reduce the risk of fungal blights common to junipers in humid climates, and shear lightly if a more formal shape is desired, though the naturally symmetrical form rarely needs heavy correction.

common_name: Spartan Juniper (Dense Columnar Privacy Screen Conifer)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Spartan's narrow, dense, columnar growth makes it one of the most popular junipers for tight privacy screens along property lines.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, spacing plants for a solid living wall as they mature; Spartan is a fast-growing, densely branched, narrow columnar juniper with rich dark green foliage that holds its color through winter better than many junipers, making it a top choice for tall, formal privacy screens and property-line hedges. It grows considerably faster than many upright conifers while staying tightly clothed with foliage from top to bottom, reducing the need for extensive shearing to maintain density. Give it full sun and good air movement to minimize fungal blight problems, and water regularly during the first one to two years to establish a strong root system, after which it becomes quite drought tolerant.

common_name: Little Ollie Dwarf Olive (Fruitless Compact Landscape Olive)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Little Ollie sets little to no fruit, avoiding the mess and staining that full-sized fruiting olives can cause near patios and walkways.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Little Ollie is a compact, naturally dwarf, non-fruiting selection of common olive, prized for the same fine-textured, silvery-gray evergreen foliage as full-sized olive trees but on a dense, easily maintained shrub that fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and containers far better than a full-scale olive tree. Because it produces little or no fruit, it avoids the dropped-olive mess and staining that can be a drawback of ornamental fruiting olives planted near hardscape. It is extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soils, and needs only occasional shearing to maintain a tidy, rounded form, making it a low-maintenance evergreen backbone plant for xeriscape and Mediterranean-style landscapes.

common_name: Dragon Lady Holly (Narrow Pyramidal Hybrid Holly)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped hollies in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Dragon Lady is a female cultivar and needs a male holly pollinator nearby, such as Blue Prince or China Boy, for reliable berry set.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Dragon Lady is a narrow, densely pyramidal hybrid holly with glossy, deep green, spiny-margined foliage and, when pollinated, a heavy crop of bright red berries that persist through winter and provide food for songbirds. Its tight, upright, formal shape needs little pruning to maintain, making it a popular choice for narrow screens, foundation accents, and formal entryway plantings where a broader holly would not fit. Give it consistent moisture while establishing, and plant a compatible male holly cultivar nearby to ensure the female flowers set fruit, since Dragon Lady itself produces only female flowers.

common_name: Robin Holly (Bronze-Red New Growth Screening Holly)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped hollies in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Robin is a female cultivar and needs a male holly pollinator nearby for the heaviest berry production.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Robin is a pyramidal hybrid holly notable for the striking bronze-red flush of its new spring growth, which matures to glossy dark green and contrasts attractively with the bright red berries produced later in the season when a compatible male holly is planted nearby for pollination. Its dense, upright form and moderate size make it a versatile choice for screening, hedging, and specimen use in the landscape, requiring only occasional shaping to maintain a neat outline. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil types once established, and consistent watering during the first couple of seasons speeds root establishment.
